title: Computability of graph Shannon capacity
formal: Does there exist one deterministic Turing machine A such that, for every finite simple undirected graph G and every integer \(k\ge 1, A\) on input \((G,k)\) halts and outputs integers a and \(b>0\) with |\(a/b- \Theta (G)|\le 2^{- k}\)? No bound on running time is imposed.
why: Asks whether a finite zero-error communication model has an effectively approximable asymptotic information rate.

progress.text: Alon–Lubetzky demonstrate large later increases beyond arbitrarily long fixed prefixes of the independence series.
A primary paper on spectral bounds explicitly states that general Shannon capacity is not known to be computable.
New special-family values and connected examples of finite-power nonattainment are published; they do not decide general effective approximation.

definitions: Encode G with vertices \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 0\), by n and its symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix; encode k, a and b as signed or unsigned binary integers as appropriate. For \(m\ge 1\), the strong power \(G^{\boxtimes m}\) has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}^{m}\). Distinct tuples x,y are adjacent exactly when, for every coordinate j, either \(x_{j}=y_{j}\) or \(\{x_{j},y_{j}\}\) is an edge of G. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; \(\alpha (H)\) is its maximum cardinality, with \(\alpha\) of the graph with no vertices equal to zero. Define \(\Theta(G)=\sup_{m\ge1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes m})^{1/m}\). For nonempty G the supremum equals the limit as \(m\to \infty\), and \(1\le \Theta (G)\le n\); set \(\Theta (G)=0\) when \(n=0\). The desired output approximates \(\Theta\) itself, not its logarithm. The same machine must work for all graphs and precision requests, with no oracle or graph-dependent advice. It may use arbitrarily much finite time and memory on each input.
answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a single algorithm and proves termination and the stated absolute-error bound for every valid graph and precision. A negative answer proves that no such uniform algorithm exists. Hardness of exact independent-set computation, failure of a particular approximation scheme, or failure of any finite power to attain the limit does not by itself answer this computability question.

context_blocks.title: Zero-error communication as a graph
context_blocks.text: Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

context_blocks.title: Why longer blocks matter
context_blocks.text: A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity \(\sqrt{5}\). For nonempty graphs, \(\log _{2}\Theta (G)\) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

context_blocks.title: A limit needs an effective error guarantee
context_blocks.text: Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

context_blocks.title: Recent progress and the scope of the question
context_blocks.text: The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of \(C_{7}\) is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.

context_blocks.title: Additional source and scope
context_blocks.text: This source raises the computability of graph Shannon capacity. The retained target asks for a uniform halting procedure at arbitrary requested precision, not just one fixed numerical tolerance.

sentences: A graph records which transmitted symbols can be confused.
Its Shannon capacity is the limiting number of distinguishable messages per use when arbitrarily long blocks are allowed.
The question asks for one terminating algorithm that approximates this quantity to any requested absolute accuracy on every finite graph.
Known examples show that fixed finite prefixes and finite-power attainment do not supply a general stopping guarantee.
The target concerns computability itself, with no required running-time bound.

context:
Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity \(\sqrt{5}\). For nonempty graphs, \(\log _{2}\Theta (G)\) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of \(C_{7}\) is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.

This source raises the computability of graph Shannon capacity. The retained target asks for a uniform halting procedure at arbitrary requested precision, not just one fixed numerical tolerance.
